checks: For B+sA the support derivative is exactly h_A uniformly, so the accepted whole-volume derivative gives dX₁. Each surface-area atom is at v_i/||v_i||, with facet area divided by ||v_i|| equal to db/(d+1) by the centroid pyramid formula. This gives dX₁=ΣP_i−db without requiring individual P_i>0.

Verified the cited Alexandrov–Fenchel Theorem 1.1. With A and B in the two distinguished slots and j−1 copies of A plus d−j−1 of B elsewhere it gives X_j²≥X_(j−1)X_(j+1). All coefficients are positive for full-dimensional convex bodies.

Interpolation of the logarithms on indices 1 to d gives X_j≥X₁(a/X₁)^((j−1)/(d−1)). The binomial sum at s=1 then gives b+X₁[(1+r)^d−1]/r. Scaling the actual inclusion (A+B)/2⊆K gives the upper comparison 2^d k.
For d=3 the binomial sum is 3X₁+3sqrt(aX₁)+a. With X=3X₁ this is X+sqrt(3aX)+a. These are the exact constants and scope in b69ebda3a2e6d72a §8 (18)–(20).

dependencies.hypotheses: Take both branches equal to the compact convex path B+sA. The initial B is full dimensional and h_A is continuous, with no remainder in the uniform support expansion.
The theorem applies in dimension d≥2 to the convex bodies A and B and the remaining d−2 copies used in the mixed-volume log-concavity inequality.
dependencies.reference: Yair Shenfeld and Ramon van Handel, Mixed volumes and the Bochner method, Theorem 1.1

overlap.comparison: Gives the underlying general first variation. It does not combine the simplex support sum with Alexandrov–Fenchel to bound the whole Minkowski sum in terms of this first coefficient.

readability: The stated hypotheses and proof scope are clear.
review_method: Independent mathematical proof review of the frozen normalized candidate
summary: The first simplex mixed coefficient and log-concavity of the mixed-volume sequence imply the stated global binomial lower bound.
